blocks.title: Water cycle
blocks.md: Water moves in a **cycle**. The Sun warms water in seas, rivers and lakes. Water turns into a gas called **water vapour**: this is **evaporation**. The vapour rises, cools and turns into tiny drops that make **clouds**: this is **condensation**.

blocks.caption: Steps of the water cycle.
blocks.alt: Four boxes: evaporation, condensation, rain, rivers to the sea.

blocks.title: Rain
blocks.md: When the drops in clouds get big and heavy, they fall as **rain**. Rain runs into streams and rivers and goes back to the sea. Then the cycle starts again.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Evaporation needs heat from the Sun.
- Clouds are made of tiny drops of water, not smoke.
- The water does not get used up; it moves round.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: What happens to sea water when the Sun warms it?

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: What forms when water vapour cools?

reviewNotes: Boiling point 100 degrees Celsius and freezing point 0 are for pure water at sea level; kept simple.

blocks.title: States of matter
blocks.md: Everything is made of **matter**. Matter can be a **solid**, a **liquid** or a **gas**. A solid keeps its shape (stone, wood). A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container (water, oil). A gas spreads out to fill space (air, steam).

blocks.caption: Changes of state.
blocks.alt: Four boxes: melting, freezing, boiling, condensing.

blocks.title: Changes
blocks.md: **Melting**: solid → liquid (ice melts). **Freezing**: liquid → solid (water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius). **Evaporating** or **boiling**: liquid → gas (water boils at 100 degrees Celsius). **Condensing**: gas → liquid.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Steam is a gas (water vapour); the white cloud we see is tiny drops.
- Air is matter too: it takes up space.
- Be careful with hot water and boiling liquids.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Ice melts in the sun. What state change is this?
steps: It becomes water, a liquid: melting.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Is oil a solid, a liquid or a gas?

blocks.title: Forces
blocks.md: A **force** is a **push** or a **pull**. Forces can make things start to move, stop, go faster or slower, or change direction. We measure force in **newtons** (you do not need to learn this yet).

blocks.caption: Forces.
blocks.alt: Four boxes about push, pull, friction and gravity.

blocks.title: Friction and gravity
blocks.md: **Friction** is a force when two things rub together. It slows things down. Rough surfaces have more friction than smooth ones. **Gravity** pulls things down towards the Earth. That is why a dropped ball falls.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Friction is not always bad: it stops our shoes from slipping.
- Heavier things are pulled down by gravity with a bigger force, but all things fall to the ground.
- Pushing and pulling are both forces.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: You open a door by pulling the handle. What force is it?
steps: You bring the door towards you.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Why does a ball roll further on a smooth floor than on grass?
steps: There is less friction on a smooth floor.

blocks.title: Light
blocks.md: **Light** lets us see. Sources of light: the **Sun**, a **fire**, a **lamp**, a **torch**. The Moon does not make light: it reflects the Sun's light. Light travels in **straight lines**.

blocks.caption: A shadow forms behind an object.
blocks.alt: A yellow light, an orange object and a grey shadow behind it.

blocks.title: Shadows
blocks.md: A **shadow** forms when an **opaque** object (one that light cannot pass through) blocks light. **Transparent** things (glass) let light through. **Translucent** things (tracing paper) let some through. Shadows are longest in the early morning and late afternoon, and shortest at midday.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- A shadow is not an object; it is the absence of light.
- Never look straight at the Sun.
- Shadows point away from the light.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Which of these makes a shadow: a wooden board or clear glass?
steps: The wooden board makes a shadow.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: At what time of day is a shadow shortest?
steps: The Sun is high in the sky.

blocks.title: Magnets
blocks.md: A **magnet** attracts things made of **iron** or **steel**, such as nails, pins and paper clips. It does not attract wood, plastic, glass or paper. Magnets can be bar-shaped, horseshoe-shaped or round.

blocks.caption: A bar magnet with N and S poles.
blocks.alt: A bar magnet with a red north end and a blue south end.

blocks.title: Poles
blocks.md: A magnet has two **poles**: **north** and **south**. **Opposite poles attract** (N and S). **Like poles repel** (N and N, or S and S). A magnet pulls strongest at its poles.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Magnets do not attract all metals. Aluminium, copper and gold are not attracted.
- Keep magnets away from phones, cards and screens.
- Like poles push apart.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Will a magnet pick up a plastic ruler?

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Two north poles are brought together. What happens?
